Randomness and Structure

The Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma

data.text/markdown: An Introduction to MNIST
We start by considering the MNIST dataset-- a large dataset of handwritten digits. The images are black and white, centered to fit in a ||(28 \times 28||) bounding box.
Really, we may view these as elements of ||(\mathbb{R}^{28 \times 28} \cong \mathbb{R}^{784}||).

How can a computer figure out which "class" of digits a given picture corresponds to? Intuitively, we expect the relative activations of a pixel to be similar. Does Euclidean distance capture this notion? In some sense, yes-- the closest neighbors usually correspond to the appropriate digit class.

data.text/html: ||(10/10||) neighbors share the query label. Distances are computed from normalized pixel intensities.

data.text/markdown: This isn't to say that we can make a good classifier just by considering the Euclidean distance. Just that, among other things, it does carry some important semantic information that we may be interested in preserving.
Dimensionality Reduction

Suppose we have very stringent computational or storage requirements that make working in a high-dimensional space untenable. How should we resolve it? This calls for some dimensionality reduction! For this to be any useful, we must preserve structures of the dataset that corresponds to the semantic information we care about. It is hard to ascertain what this structure exactly is (let alone decide how we can "preserve" it)-- for this talk, we use Euclidean distances as a proxy motivated by our prior investigations. Note that MNIST is being used here just as a toy example, the regime where high-dimensional spaces become a practical issue is really when we get to millions of dimensions.

More formally, we want a map ||(P: \mathbb{R}^{d} \to \mathbb{R}^{k}||), where ||(d = 784||) and ||(k \ll d||), such that ||[ \lVert P\mathbf{x}^{(i)}-P\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2 \approx \lVert \mathbf{x}^{(i)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2 ||]for every pair of points in our dataset.
Given access to the dataset, PCA is the natural solution. It learns a subspace optimized for MNIST. Can we choose the map before inspecting the data and still preserve its pairwise geometry?

Choose ||(P \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}||) independently of the data, with ||[ P_{ab} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\frac{1}{k}\right), \qquad \mathbf{x} \longmapsto P\mathbf{x}. ||]Seemingly we haven't even considered the contents of the MNIST dataset. Why should it work at all?

data.text/html: The same ||(3{,}500||) pairs appear in both panels. PCA is globally rescaled to preserve total variance; the Gaussian map is chosen without inspecting MNIST.

The Gaussian row uses the Moore--Penrose reconstruction ||(P^\dagger P\mathbf{x}||); the PCA row uses ||(\boldsymbol{\mu}+U_kU_k^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})||). PCA is optimized for this reconstruction task, while JL concerns distances in ||(\mathbb R^k||).

data.text/markdown: The Gaussian random projection works surprisingly well despite not using any of the data itself. To understand why, forget the whole dataset and fix one nonzero vector ||(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d||). We first ask what the projection does to ||(\lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert_2||).

||[ \begin{aligned} P &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & & \vert\\ \mathbf{p}^{(1)} & \mathbf{p}^{(2)} & \cdots & \mathbf{p}^{(d)}\\ \vert & \vert & & \vert \end{bmatrix}, &\qquad (P\mathbf{v})_j=\sum_{i=1}^d P_{ji}v_i,\\[4pt] \mathbb E[(P\mathbf{v})_j^2] &=\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2\,\mathbb E[P_{ji}^2] =\frac{\lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2}{k},\\[4pt] \mathbb E[\lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2] &=\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb E[(P\mathbf{v})_j^2] =\lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2. \end{aligned} ||]The cross terms vanish because the entries of ||(P||) are independent and have mean zero.

The matrix defined by ||(P_{ji}\sim\mathcal N(0,1/k)||) preserves squared norm in expectation. We can even quantitatively show that ||(\lVert P v \rVert_2^2||) remain close to ||(\lVert v \rVert_2^2||).

data.text/html: For a fixed ||(\mathbf{v}||), ||(\lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2 / \lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2 \sim \chi^2_{25}/25||). Its mean is ||(1||).

data.text/markdown: We will use the following concentration inequality without proving it. For every fixed nonzero ||(\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb R^d||) and ||(0<\epsilon<1||), ||[ \Pr\!\left[ \left| \frac{\lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2} {\lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2}-1 \right|>\epsilon \right] \leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{k\epsilon^2}{8}\right). ||]Here ||(\epsilon||) is the squared-distance distortion we tolerate. The important feature is that the probability of failure for one fixed vector decreases exponentially in ||(k\epsilon^2||).

data.text/html:
1. Reduce to a chi-squared random variable

For a fixed nonzero vector ||(\mathbf{v}||), define ||[ g_j=\frac{\sqrt{k}(P\mathbf{v})_j} {\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert_2}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,k. ||]Each ||(g_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1)||), and the ||(g_j||) are independent because they come from independent rows of ||(P||). Consequently, ||[ Z:=\sum_{j=1}^k g_j^2 =\frac{k\lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2} {\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert_2^2} \sim\chi_k^2. ||]

2. Compute the MGF

If ||(g\sim\mathcal N(0,1)||) and ||(\lambda<1/2||), then ||[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[e^{\lambda g^2}] &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\lambda t^2}e^{-t^2/2}\,dt\\ &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-(1-2\lambda)t^2/2}\,dt\\ &=(1-2\lambda)^{-1/2}. \end{aligned} ||]The last equality is the Gaussian integral after the change of variables ||(u=\sqrt{1-2\lambda}\,t||). Independence now gives ||[ \mathbb E[e^{\lambda Z}] =\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb E[e^{\lambda g_j^2}] =(1-2\lambda)^{-k/2}. ||]

3. Optimize the upper tail

For ||(0<\lambda<1/2||), Markov's inequality gives ||[ \begin{aligned} \Pr[Z\geq k(1+\epsilon)] &=\Pr[e^{\lambda Z} \geq e^{\lambda k(1+\epsilon)}]\\ &\leq e^{-\lambda k(1+\epsilon)} (1-2\lambda)^{-k/2}. \end{aligned} ||]Taking logarithms turns the right-hand side into ||[ \phi_+(\lambda) =-\lambda k(1+\epsilon) -\frac{k}{2}\log(1-2\lambda). ||]Its derivative vanishes when ||[ \phi_+'(\lambda) =-k(1+\epsilon)+\frac{k}{1-2\lambda}=0, \qquad \lambda_*=\frac{\epsilon}{2(1+\epsilon)}. ||]Since ||(\phi_+''(\lambda)=2k/(1-2\lambda)^2>0||), this is the minimizer. Moreover, ||(1-2\lambda_*=1/(1+\epsilon)||). Using ||(\log(1/u)=-\log u||), ||[ \begin{aligned} \phi_+(\lambda_*) &=-\frac{k\epsilon}{2} -\frac{k}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\right)\\ &=-\frac{k}{2} \bigl(\epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon)\bigr). \end{aligned} ||]Therefore ||[ \Pr[Z\geq k(1+\epsilon)] \leq \exp\!\left[-\frac{k}{2} \bigl(\epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon)\bigr)\right]. ||]

4. Optimize the lower tail

For ||(t>0||), apply Markov's inequality to ||(e^{-tZ}||): ||[ \Pr[Z\leq k(1-\epsilon)] \leq e^{tk(1-\epsilon)}(1+2t)^{-k/2}. ||]The logarithm of this bound is ||[ \phi_-(t)=tk(1-\epsilon) -\frac{k}{2}\log(1+2t). ||]Differentiating and setting the derivative to zero gives ||[ \phi_-'(t) =k(1-\epsilon)-\frac{k}{1+2t}=0, \qquad t_*=\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}, \qquad 1+2t_*=\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}. ||]Since ||(\phi_-''(t)=2k/(1+2t)^2>0||), this is the minimizer. Thus, using ||(\log(1/u)=-\log u||), ||[ \begin{aligned} \phi_-(t_*) &=\frac{k\epsilon}{2} -\frac{k}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}\right)\\ &=-\frac{k}{2} \bigl(-\epsilon-\log(1-\epsilon)\bigr), \end{aligned} ||]and hence ||[ \Pr[Z\leq k(1-\epsilon)] \leq \exp\!\left[-\frac{k}{2} \bigl(-\epsilon-\log(1-\epsilon)\bigr)\right]. ||]

5. Simplify the logarithmic terms

For ||(0<\epsilon<1||), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives ||[ \begin{aligned} \epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon) &=\int_0^\epsilon\frac{s}{1+s}\,ds \geq\int_0^\epsilon\frac{s}{2}\,ds =\frac{\epsilon^2}{4},\\[4pt] -\epsilon-\log(1-\epsilon) &=\int_0^\epsilon\frac{s}{1-s}\,ds \geq\int_0^\epsilon s\,ds =\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}. \end{aligned} ||]Substituting these inequalities yields ||[ \Pr[Z\geq k(1+\epsilon)]\leq e^{-k\epsilon^2/8}, \qquad \Pr[Z\leq k(1-\epsilon)]\leq e^{-k\epsilon^2/4}. ||]Finally, adding the two tail probabilities gives ||[ \Pr\!\left[ \left|\frac{Z}{k}-1\right|>\epsilon \right] \leq e^{-k\epsilon^2/8}+e^{-k\epsilon^2/4} \leq 2e^{-k\epsilon^2/8}. ||]We used the standard identities ||(\log(a^r)=r\log a||) and ||(\log(1/u)=-\log u||); the integral identities above are what turn the exact Chernoff exponents into the simpler ||(e^{-\Theta(k\epsilon^2)}||) form.

data.text/markdown: For each pair of data points ||(i<j||), define the difference vector ||[ \mathbf{v}^{(i,j)}=\mathbf{x}^{(i)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}. ||]Since ||(P||) is linear, ||[ \lVert P\mathbf{x}^{(i)}-P\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2 =\lVert P(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\rVert_2 =\lVert P\mathbf{v}^{(i,j)}\rVert_2. ||]Therefore, preserving every pairwise distance is exactly the problem of preserving the norms of all the difference vectors ||(\mathbf{v}^{(i,j)}||). There are ||[ m=\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2 ||]of them. Notice that this is a finite list fixed before we sample ||(P||).

Let ||(B^{(i,j)}||) be the event that the distance between ||(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}||) and ||(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}||) is distorted by more than ||(\epsilon||). The union bound says ||[ \Pr\!\left[\text{at least one pair fails}\right] =\Pr\!\left[\bigcup_{i<j}B^{(i,j)}\right] \leq\sum_{i<j}\Pr[B^{(i,j)}]. ||]

Combining our prior result with the union bound then gives us. ||[ \Pr[\text{at least one pair fails}] \leq 2\binom n2\exp\!\left(-\frac{k\epsilon^2}{8}\right). ||]To make this at most ||(\delta||), it is enough to choose ||[ k\geq \frac{8}{\epsilon^2} \log\!\left(\frac{2\binom n2}{\delta}\right) =O\!\left(\frac{\log(n/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}\right). ||]There are quadratically many "bad events", but the probability decays exponentially in ||(k||).
Johnson--Lindenstrauss Lemma

Let ||(\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{x}^{(n)}\in\mathbb R^d||) and ||(0<\epsilon,\delta<1||). If ||[ P_{ab}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1/k) \qquad\text{and}\qquad k\geq C\epsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta), ||]then, with probability at least ||(1-\delta||), every pair ||(i<j||) satisfies ||[ (1-\epsilon)\lVert \mathbf{x}^{(i)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2^2 \leq \lVert P\mathbf{x}^{(i)}-P\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2^2 \leq (1+\epsilon)\lVert \mathbf{x}^{(i)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\rVert_2^2. ||]
